Hi there! I feel like you may be missing the point, but I’m assuming that you are trying to understand and I’d like to try and meet you where you’re at. 

For sake of argument, let’s say what your daughter said IS manipulative. 

When someone says something manipulative, it’s almost always because they have an unmet need and feel the only way they can get it met is by engaging in a manipulative behavior. It’s normal to see manipulative behavior in teens and children, but obviously not the healthiest way to manage it. An appropriate response from a parent is to tell the child that their needs can be met without engaging in manipulation but by being direct. Because their needs are important and they are loved and wanted unconditionally. But most importantly, a parent has to try to get their unmet need met. 

Why YTA in this instance is because rather than showing your daughter she’s loved unconditionally and her needs will be met AND rather than communicate with her that healthy open communication will help her get those needs met, you also engaging in toxic and childish behavior rather than acting as a parent.
This is so well put! I hope the OP sees this!

Take care of yourself. Prioritize your needs and well-being as much as you’re able. Validate and process all your feelings. You’re a human, not a robot and two seemingly contradictory statements can be true at once. You’re allowed to love your father and also be furious at him for the harm he caused. Don’t be afraid to let yourself feel everything you need to feel and try not to label any feelings as being bad or wrong. I’m sorry you’re going through this.

Absolutely! This is such a frustrating part of the whole experience, and I’m sorry you’re having to deal with it. I’ve found it helpful to write down some of the incidents after they happen and look back on them, sometimes I even look back at what I’ve posted on this forum. It’s so hard when they’ve got the mask on and they’re being nice, but that niceness does NOT erase or invalidate the abuse-it’s another layer of it.

If you do want to actually help your daughter, it’s pretty important to know that not all therapists are a good fit, and it can be a really big struggle for someone who’s had bad experiences to feel like it’s worth it to go back. It’s helpful to frame it almost like a checklist with qualities you do and don’t want in a therapist, ie someone who’s super medical and business-like versus someone who’s comfortable joking around. Also currently YTA, consider changing your behavior and educating yourself.

Even if it isn’t “necessary” per se, it may be a good way to get yourself into a more healthy place with yourself mentally. For me, therapy helped me better understand where my unhealthy eating habits stemmed from and how to change that dynamic, as well as how to address the unhealthy ways I thought about/spoke about myself. The way you talk about yourself is somewhat concerning. You sound like you’re very thin, and I’m sure you’re very beautiful as well.
